questions.knowledge_point: Finding the First Terms of the Taylor Series of a Function About a Point
questions.problem: Find the first three non-zero terms in the Taylor expansion of $\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)$ about the point $x=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
We use Taylor's theorem in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+\frac{{f}^{‴}(a)}{3!}(x-a)^{3}+⋯,
$$

with $f(x)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡x$ and $a=1.$ 

Computing the required derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡x \\ f(1) & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡1=\frac{\pi }{4} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}} \\ {f}^{′}(1) & =\frac{1}{1+1}=\frac{1}{2} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\frac{2x}{(1+{x}^{2})^{2}} \\ {f}^{″}(1) & =-\frac{2(1)}{(1+1)^{2}}=-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{arctan}⁡x & =\frac{\pi }{4}+(\frac{1}{2})(x-1)+\frac{1}{2!}(-\frac{1}{2})(x-1)^{2}+⋯ \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}+\frac{1}{2}(x-1)-\frac{1}{4}(x-1)^{2}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the First Terms of the Taylor Series of a Function About a Point
questions.worked_solution:
We use Taylor's formula in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+\frac{{f}^{‴}(a)}{3!}(x-a)^{3}+⋯,
$$

with $f(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and $a=-\frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

Computing the required derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ f\,(-\frac{\pi }{2}) & =sin\,(-\frac{\pi }{2})=-1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}\,(-\frac{\pi }{2}) & =cos\,(-\frac{\pi }{2})=0 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{″}\,(-\frac{\pi }{2}) & =-sin\,(-\frac{\pi }{2})=1 \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{‴}\,(-\frac{\pi }{2}) & =-cos\,(-\frac{\pi }{2})=0 \\ {f}^{(4)}(x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{(4)}\,(-\frac{\pi }{2}) & =sin\,(-\frac{\pi }{2})=-1. \\ \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =-1+0\,(x+\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{1}{2!}\,{(x+\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2}+\frac{0}{3!}\,{(x+\frac{\pi }{2})}^{3}+\frac{(-1)}{4!}\,{(x+\frac{\pi }{2})}^{4}+⋯ \\  & =-1+\frac{1}{2}\,{(x+\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2}-\frac{1}{24}\,{(x+\frac{\pi }{2})}^{4}+⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Approximating the Value of a Function at a  Point Using Its Taylor Series
questions.worked_solution:
We use Taylor's formula in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+⋯,
$$

with $f(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and $a=2\pi .$ 

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ f(2\pi ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi )=1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(2\pi ) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )=0 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{″}(2\pi ) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi )=-1 \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{‴}(2\pi ) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )=0 \\ {f}^{(4)}(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{(4)}(2\pi ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi )=1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Taylor series is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =(1)+(0)(x-2\pi )+\frac{(-1)}{2!}(x-2\pi )^{2}+\frac{(0)}{3!}(x-2\pi )^{3}+\frac{(1)}{4!}(x-2\pi )^{4}+⋯ \\  & =1-\frac{(x-2\pi )^{2}}{2}+\frac{(x-2\pi )^{4}}{24}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=5$ into the above to approximate $\operatorname{cos}⁡(5).$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5) & ≈1-\frac{(5-2\pi )^{2}}{2}+\frac{(5-2\pi )^{4}}{24} \\  & ≈0.29,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

questions.knowledge_point: Approximating the Value of a Function at a  Point Using Its Taylor Series
questions.worked_solution:
We use Taylor's formula in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+⋯,
$$

with $f(x)={2}^{x}$ and $a=2.$ 

Computing the required derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={2}^{x} \\ f(2) & =4 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & ={2}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ {f}^{′}(2) & =4\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & ={2}^{x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)^{2} \\ {f}^{″}(2) & =4(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Taylor expansion is

$$
{2}^{x}=4+4(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)(x-2)+\frac{4(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)^{2}}{2!}(x-2)^{2}+⋯,
$$

which simplifies to

$$
{2}^{x}=4+4(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)(x-2)+2(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)^{2}(x-2)^{2}+⋯.
$$

We substitute $x=2.1.$ Since $2.1-2=0.1=\frac{1}{10},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{2.1} & ≈4+4(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)(\frac{1}{10})+2(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)^{2}{(\frac{1}{10})}^{2} \\  & ≈4.29.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{2}^{2.1}≈4.29.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Approximating the Value of a Function at a  Point Using Its Taylor Series
questions.worked_solution:
We use Taylor's formula in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+⋯,
$$

with $f(x)={5}^{x}$ and $a=1.$ 

Computing the required derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={5}^{x} \\ f(1) & =5 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & ={5}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡5 \\ {f}^{′}(1) & =5\operatorname{ln}⁡5 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & ={5}^{x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡5)^{2} \\ {f}^{″}(1) & =5(\operatorname{ln}⁡5)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Taylor expansion is

$$
{5}^{x}=5+5(\operatorname{ln}⁡5)(x-1)+\frac{5(\operatorname{ln}⁡5)^{2}}{2!}(x-1)^{2}+⋯,
$$

which simplifies to

$$
{5}^{x}=5+5(\operatorname{ln}⁡5)(x-1)+\frac{5(\operatorname{ln}⁡5)^{2}}{2}(x-1)^{2}+⋯.
$$

We substitute $x=1.3.$ Since $1.3-1=0.3=\frac{3}{10},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{5}^{1.3} & ≈5+5(\operatorname{ln}⁡5)(\frac{3}{10})+\frac{5(\operatorname{ln}⁡5)^{2}}{2}{(\frac{3}{10})}^{2} \\  & ≈8.0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{5}^{1.3}≈8.0.
$$
